'''Emily Ann Carter'''<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Carter |first=Emily Ann |title=Finesse in Quantum Chemistry: Accurate Energetics Relevant for Reaction Mechanisms |date=1987 |degree=phd |publisher=California Institute of Technology |url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechETD:etd-11212003-111159 |language=en}}</ref> is the Gerhard R. Andlinger Professor in Energy and the Environment and a professor of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering (MAE), the Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment (ACEE), and Applied and Computational Mathematics at [[Princeton University]]. She is also a member of the executive management team at the [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory]] (PPPL), serving as Senior Strategic Advisor and Associate Laboratory Director for Applied Materials and Sustainability Sciences.

The author of over 475 publications and patents, Carter has delivered over 600 invited and plenary lectures worldwide and has served on advisory boards spanning a wide range of disciplines. Among other honors, Carter is an elected foreign member of [[Royal Society|The Royal Society]] (2024), and fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry (2022), the [[National Academy of Inventors]] (2014), the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2008), the [[Institute of Physics]] (2004), [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (2000), the [[American Vacuum Society]] (1995),<ref name="AVS">{{cite web |title=Society Honors |url=https://avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Society-Honors/Fellow-of-the-Society |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160314034305/http://avs.org/Awards-Recognition/Society-Honors/Fellow-of-the-Society |archive-date=14 March 2016 |access-date=21 March 2016 |website=AVS}}</ref> the [[American Physical Society]] (1994),<ref name="CG" />  and the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=ACS Fellows Program - American Chemical Society |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/fellows.html |access-date=2016-10-11 |website=American Chemical Society}}</ref> She is also an elected member of the European Academy of Sciences (2020), the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (2016),<ref name="NAE2016">{{cite web |title=NAE Members |url=https://www.nae.edu/149850.aspx |access-date=21 March 2016 |website=National Academy of Engineering}}</ref> [[International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science]] (2009),<ref name="Emery">{{cite web |last1=Emery |first1=Chris |date=July 29, 2009 |title=Carter elected to International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science |url=https://www.princeton.edu/engineering/news/archive/?id=1035 |access-date=21 March 2016 |website=Princeton University}}</ref><ref name="Inventors">{{cite web |title=Aksay, Carter named National Academy of Inventors Fellows |url=https://www.princeton.edu/research/news/archive/index.xml?id=14141 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160409165708/http://www.princeton.edu/research/news/archive/index.xml?id=14141 |archive-date=9 April 2016 |access-date=26 March 2016 |website=Princeton University}}</ref> the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (2008).<ref name="PNAS">{{cite web |title=Podcast Interview: Emily Carter |url=http://www.pnas.org/site/misc/Cartertranscript.pdf |access-date=21 March 2016 |website=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences}}</ref>

==Biography==
Emily Carter received a Bachelor of Science in chemistry from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], in 1982 (graduating Phi Beta Kappa). She earned her [[PhD]] in physical chemistry in 1987 from the [[California Institute of Technology]], where she worked with [[William Andrew Goddard III]], studying [[Homogeneous catalysis|homogeneous]] and [[heterogeneous catalysis]].<ref name="thesis-carter-1987">{{cite thesis |url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechETD:etd-11212003-111159 |title=Finesse In Quantum Chemistry: Accurate Energetics Relevant for Reaction Mechanisms |date=1987 |institution=California Institute of Technology |degree=PhD |last=Carter |first=Emily Ann |id={{ProQuest|303459467}} |oclc=1014494990}}</ref><ref name=CG>{{cite web|url=https://carter.princeton.edu/|title=The Carter Group|publisher=[[Princeton University]]|access-date=23 October 2015}}</ref><ref name="CV">{{cite web|title=Emily Ann Carter|url=https://carter.princeton.edu/files/2016/03/EAC_CV_March-14-2016.pdf|website=Princeton University|access-date=26 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160409150310/https://carter.princeton.edu/files/2016/03/EAC_CV_March-14-2016.pdf|archive-date=9 April 2016}}</ref> During her postdoc at the [[University of Colorado, Boulder]], she worked with James T. Hynes carrying out studies on the dynamics of (photo-induced) electron transfer in solution. She also worked with James Hynes, [[Giovanni Ciccotti]], and Ray Kapral to develop the widely used Blue Moon ensemble, a rare-event sampling method for condensed matter simulations.<ref name="Carter">{{cite journal |last1=Carter |first1=E.A. |last2=Ciccotti |first2=Giovanni |last3=Hynes |first3=James T. |last4=Kapral |first4=Raymond |date=April 1989 |title=Constrained reaction coordinate dynamics for the simulation of rare events |url=https://carter.princeton.edu/files/2015/08/EAC-019.pdf |journal=Chemical Physics Letters |volume=156 |issue=5 |pages=472–477 |bibcode=1989CPL...156..472C |doi=10.1016/S0009-2614(89)87314-2 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160409134025/https://carter.princeton.edu/files/2015/08/EAC-019.pdf |archive-date=2016-04-09 |access-date=2016-03-26}}</ref><ref name="Hynes">{{cite journal |date=January 2008 |title=Autobiography of James T. (Casey) Hynes |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |volume=112 |issue=2 |pages=191–194 |doi=10.1021/jp710517n}}</ref><ref name="Madsen">{{cite book |last1=Madsen |first1=Lynnette |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bVhwCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA29 |title=Successful women in ceramics and glass science and engineering |date=2014 |publisher=John Wiley |isbn=978-1-118-73360-8 |location=[S.l.] |pages=29–36 |access-date=21 March 2016}}</ref>

From 1988 to 2004, she held professorships in chemistry and materials science and engineering at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]]. During those years, she was the Dr. Lee's visiting research fellow in the Sciences at [[Christ Church, Oxford]] (1996), a visiting scholar in the department of physics at [[Harvard University]] (1999), and a visiting associate in aeronautics at the [[California Institute of Technology]] (2001). She moved to [[Princeton University]] in 2004.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Emily A. Carter |url=https://dof.princeton.edu/people/emily-carter |access-date=2024-01-29 |website=Office of the Dean of the Faculty |language=en}}</ref> In 2006, she was named Arthur W. Marks '19 Professor. From 2009 to 2014, she was co-director of the Department of Energy Frontier Research Center on Combustion Science. She became the founding director of the Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment in 2010, [[Gerhard Andlinger|Gerhard R. Andlinger]] Professor in 2011, and dean of the school of engineering and applied science in 2016.<ref name="CG" /> After a national search, Prof. Carter served from 2016 to 2019 as Dean of the [[Princeton University School of Engineering and Applied Science]]<ref name=":0" /> and the Gerhard R. Andlinger Professor in Energy and the Environment. She was also a professor in the department of [https://mae.princeton.edu/people/faculty/carter mechanical and aerospace engineering] and the Program in Applied and Computational Mathematics at [[Princeton University]]. She was an associated faculty member in the Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment, the department of chemistry, the department of chemical and biological engineering, the Princeton Institute for Computational Science and Engineering (PICSciE), the [[High Meadows Environmental Institute]] (HMEI), and the Princeton Institute for the Science and Technology of Materials (PRISM). She was the founding director of the Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment from 2010 to 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Emily Carter |url=https://environmenthalfcentury.princeton.edu/experts/emily-carter |access-date=2024-01-31 |website=Princeton Environmental Research |language=en}}</ref> She served as UCLA's Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost (EVCP) from 2019 to 2021 and was Distinguished Professor of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Biography {{!}} EXECUTIVE VICE CHANCELLOR & PROVOST EMILY A. CARTER |url=https://www.evc.ucla.edu/biography |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227204356/https://www.evc.ucla.edu/biography |archive-date=2019-12-27 |access-date=2019-12-27 |website=www.evc.ucla.edu}}</ref><ref name="CV" /> She is currently a member of the executive management team at the [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory]] (PPPL), serving as Senior Strategic Advisor and Associate Laboratory Director for Applied Materials and Sustainability Sciences.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Leadership |url=https://www.pppl.gov/about/leadership |access-date=2024-01-31 |website=Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory |language=en}}</ref>

==Research==
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2y9M6f1KklE "Andlinger Center director Emily Carter lays out strategic vision for energy research"], [[Princeton University|Princeton Engineering]] | video2 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A3TXo4Ju0aU "Mechanisms of Photoelectrochemical Reduction of Carbon Dioxide"], [[Scuola Normale Superiore]] | video3 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kHTaxWpRA0U "Quantum Mechanics and the Future of the Planet"], [[Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics]] }}

Carter has made significant contributions to theoretical and [[computational chemistry]] and physics, including the development of [[Ab initio quantum chemistry methods|''ab initio'' quantum chemistry methods]],<ref name="Carter2008">{{cite journal |last1=Carter |first1=E. A. |date=8 August 2008 |title=Challenges in Modeling Materials Properties Without Experimental Input |url=http://pcss.xmu.edu.cn/old/users/xlu/group/download/modeling_materials.pdf |journal=Science |volume=321 |issue=5890 |pages=800–803 |bibcode=2008Sci...321..800C |doi=10.1126/science.1158009 |pmid=18687955 |s2cid=206512850 |access-date=26 March 2016 |archive-date=8 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408184123/http://pcss.xmu.edu.cn/old/users/xlu/group/download/modeling_materials.pdf }}</ref> methods for accurate description of molecules at the quantum level, and an algorithm for identifying transitional states in chemical reactions.<ref name="F49620">{{cite web |last1=Carter |first1=Emily A. |date=April 17, 1997 |title=Final Technical Report for AFOSR Grant No. F49620-93-1-0145 |url=http://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a325655.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408030613/http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a325655.pdf |archive-date=April 8, 2016 |access-date=26 March 2016 |website=Defense Technical Information Center}}</ref> She pioneered the combination of ''ab initio'' quantum chemistry with [[kinetic Monte Carlo|kinetic Monte Carlo simulations]] (KMC), [[molecular dynamics]] (MD), and quasi-continuum solid mechanics simulations relevant to the study of surfaces and interfaces of materials. She has extensively investigated the chemical and mechanical causes and mechanisms of failure in materials such as [[silicon]], [[germanium]], [[iron]] and [[steel]], and proposed methods for protecting materials from failure.<ref name="Madsen" />

She has developed fast methods for [[orbital-free density functional theory]] (OF-DFT) that can be applied to large numbers of atoms<ref name="Adarlo">{{cite web |last1=Adarlo |first1=Sharon |title=Emily Carter is first woman and first Princeton professor to win Hirschfelder Prize |url=https://acee.princeton.edu/news/emily-carter-is-first-woman-and-first-princeton-professor-to-win-hirschfelder-prize/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151031015028/http://acee.princeton.edu/news/emily-carter-is-first-woman-and-first-princeton-professor-to-win-hirschfelder-prize/ |archive-date=October 31, 2015 |access-date=October 28, 2015 |website=Princeton University}}</ref> as well as embedded correlated wavefunction theory for the study of local [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter]] electronic structure.<ref name="Libisch">{{cite journal |last1=Libisch |first1=Florian |last2=Huang |first2=Chen |last3=Carter |first3=Emily A. |date=16 September 2014 |title=Embedded Correlated Wavefunction Schemes: Theory and Applications |journal=Accounts of Chemical Research |volume=47 |issue=9 |pages=2768–2775 |doi=10.1021/ar500086h |pmid=24873211}}</ref><ref name="Sharifzadeh">{{cite journal |last1=Sharifzadeh |first1=Sahar |last2=Huang |first2=Patrick |last3=Carter |first3=Emily A. |date=March 2009 |title=All-electron embedded correlated wavefunction theory for condensed matter electronic structure |journal=Chemical Physics Letters |volume=470 |issue=4–6 |pages=347–352 |bibcode=2009CPL...470..347S |doi=10.1016/j.cplett.2009.01.072}}</ref> This work has relevance to the understanding of photoelectrocatalysis.<ref name="Adarlo" /><ref name="Photoelectrocatalysis">{{cite web |title=Renewable Fuels and Chemicals from Photoelectrocatalysis |url=https://www.chem.wisc.edu/content/hirschfelder-lectures-0 |access-date=26 March 2016 |website=University of Wisconsin-Madison |archive-date=8 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408011742/https://www.chem.wisc.edu/content/hirschfelder-lectures-0 }}</ref> Her current research focuses on the understanding and design of materials for [[sustainable energy]].<ref name="Madsen" /><ref name="Energy">{{cite web |title=Five Questions with Emily Carter: Seeking Sustainable Energy Solutions |url=http://giving.princeton.edu/impact-stories/five-questions-emily-carter |access-date=21 March 2016 |website=Princeton University}}</ref>  Applications include conversion of sunlight to electricity, clean and efficient use of [[biofuels]] and [[solid oxide fuel cell]]s, and development of materials for use in fuel-efficient vehicles and [[fusion reactors]].<ref name="CV" /><ref name="Kavli">{{cite web |title=Kavli Foundation Lecture Series |url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/meetings/spring-2016/program-overview/kavli-lecture-series.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160407230025/http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/meetings/spring-2016/program-overview/kavli-lecture-series.html |archive-date=7 April 2016 |access-date=26 March 2016 |website=ACS Chemistry for Life |publisher=American Chemical Society}}</ref>

Carter's research is supported by multiple grants from the U.S. Department of Defense and the Department of Energy. She was elected as a member into the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (2016) for the development of quantum chemistry computational methods for the design of molecules and materials for sustainable energy.
